title: Forces
description: Animated KS3 Physics lesson on forces for ages 9 to 14: pushes and pulls, newtons, force arrows, resultant force, balanced and unbalanced forces, mass and weight, and stretching springs.
intro: Pushes, pulls, force arrows, balanced forces, weight and springs, explained by the owl in six short parts.

steps.say: A force is a **push** or a **pull**. Here the owl is pushing a box.
Forces can make things speed up, slow down or change direction.
Forces can also change an object's shape. Squeeze a ball and it squashes.
We measure forces in **newtons**. The short way to write newtons is **N**.
We draw a force as an arrow. It points the way the force acts. A longer arrow means a bigger force: the 10 N arrow is twice as long as the 5 N arrow.

check.q: Which unit do we use to measure force?
check.hint: The unit is named after the scientist Isaac Newton.
check.explain: Forces are measured in **newtons (N)**. Kilograms measure mass, not force.

steps.say: **Contact forces** act when two things touch.
**Friction** acts where two surfaces rub together. It pushes against the way things slide.
**Air resistance** pushes back on things moving through air. Water resistance does the same in water.
**Non-contact forces** act across a gap, without touching. **Gravity** pulls the apple down to the ground.
**Magnetism** and **static electricity** are non-contact forces too. The magnet pulls the paper clip across the gap.

check.q: Which of these is a **non-contact** force?
check.hint: Which force can act without anything touching, like the Earth pulling a falling apple?
check.explain: **Gravity** acts across a gap. Friction, air resistance and water resistance all need surfaces to touch.

steps.say: Usually more than one force acts on an object. The **resultant force** is what you get when you add them all up.
Forces in the **same direction** add up. Two friends push with 5 N and 3 N. The resultant is 5 + 3 = 8 N to the right.
steps.speak: Forces in the same direction add up. Two friends push with 5 newtons and 3 newtons. The resultant is 5 plus 3, which is 8 newtons to the right.

steps.say: Forces in **opposite directions** take away. The owl pushes with 10 N and friction pulls back with 4 N.
10 − 4 = 6, so the resultant force is 6 N, in the direction of the bigger force: to the right.
steps.speak: 10 minus 4 is 6, so the resultant force is 6 newtons, in the direction of the bigger force: to the right.

check.q: A 12 N force pushes a trolley to the right and a 5 N force pushes it to the left. What is the resultant force?
check.hint: Opposite directions: take the smaller force away from the bigger one. Which way is the bigger force?
check.explain: 12 − 5 = 7, and the bigger force is to the right, so the resultant is **7 N to the right**.

steps.say: A book rests on a table. Gravity pulls it down with 5 N. The table pushes it up with 5 N.
The forces are equal and opposite, so they are **balanced**. The resultant force is zero.
Balanced forces do not change how something moves. A still object stays still, and a moving object keeps going at the same speed in the same direction.
If the forces are **unbalanced**, the motion changes. The driving force is now bigger than air resistance, so the car speeds up.
If air resistance and friction are bigger than the driving force, the car slows down.

check.q: A car moves at a steady speed in a straight line. What can you say about the forces on it?
options: There are no forces on it
check.hint: Is the car speeding up, slowing down or turning? If its motion isn't changing, what does that tell you?
check.explain: Its motion is not changing, so the forces are **balanced**: the driving force equals the resistance forces. There are still forces acting; they just cancel out.

steps.say: **Mass** is how much stuff is in an object. We measure it in kilograms, **kg**. Your mass is the same everywhere.
**Weight** is the force of gravity pulling on that mass. Weight is a force, so we measure it in newtons.
On Earth, gravity pulls about 10 N on every kilogram. So **weight = mass × 10 N/kg**. A 2 kg bag weighs 2 × 10 = 20 N.
steps.speak: On Earth, gravity pulls about 10 newtons on every kilogram. So weight equals mass times 10 newtons per kilogram. A 2 kilogram bag weighs 2 times 10, which is 20 newtons.

steps.say: Gravity on the Moon is much weaker, about 1.6 N/kg. The same bag weighs only about 3.2 N there, but its mass is still 2 kg.
steps.speak: Gravity on the Moon is much weaker, about 1.6 newtons per kilogram. The same bag weighs only about 3.2 newtons there, but its mass is still 2 kilograms.

check.q: A dog has a mass of 30 kg. What is its weight on Earth? (Use 10 N/kg.)
check.hint: Weight = mass × 10 N/kg. And weight is a force, so which unit does it use?
check.explain: 30 × 10 = 300, so the dog weighs **300 N**. Not 300 kg: weight is a force, so it is in newtons.

steps.say: Hang a weight on a spring and the spring stretches. How much longer it gets is called the **extension**.
With 1 N the spring stretches 2 cm. With 2 N it stretches 4 cm. With 3 N, 6 cm.
steps.speak: With 1 newton the spring stretches 2 centimetres. With 2 newtons it stretches 4 centimetres. With 3 newtons, 6 centimetres.

steps.say: Double the force and you double the extension. This is called **Hooke's law**.
But pull too hard and the spring is damaged: it stays stretched and doesn't go back to its old shape. Then Hooke's law stops working.

check.q: A spring stretches 3 cm when you hang 1 N on it. How far does it stretch with 4 N? (It isn't damaged.)
check.hint: 4 N is four times as big as 1 N. So the extension is four times as big too.
check.explain: 4 times the force gives 4 times the extension: 4 × 3 = **12 cm**.
